keyVerseText: Be it known unto the king, that we went into the province of Judea, to the house of the great God, which is builded with great stones, and timber is laid in the walls, and this work goeth fast on, and prospereth in their hands. great: Chaldee, stones of rolling
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word הִיא (hûwʼ) is the feminine singular form corresponding to the masculine הוּא, both pronouns meaning 'he, she, it' or 'the same.' Its root sense conveys identity and emphasis on the subject itself, often used to affirm or resume the subject in discourse. Derived from Aramaic origins, this pronoun carries the nuance of self-reference or demonstrative focus, distinguishing the subject as identical or emphatic rather than merely generic.
usageInScripture: With 22 occurrences and varied translations such as 'which was,' 'there is but one,' 'are,' and 'this,' הִיא demonstrates flexibility in Hebrew narrative and discourse. It functions both as a simple pronoun and as an idiomatic expression emphasizing existence or identity. Its usage ranges from resuming a subject with emphasis to anticipating the subject or affirming existence, revealing its integral role in clarifying and intensifying the subject within biblical texts.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding הִיא deepens our appreciation of biblical texts by highlighting the personal and emphatic nature of subjects, especially when referring to God or key figures. This pronoun underscores the reality and presence of the subject, reminding believers that biblical declarations are not abstract but refer to a living, active person or truth. In Christ-centered theology, recognizing such emphasis enriches the conviction that God is not distant but intimately involved, the very 'same' and faithful throughout Scripture. It also points to the unity and singularity of divine revelation, affirming 'there is but one' God who acts decisively in history.
keyVerseReflection: In Ezra 5:8, the phrase 'the house of the great God, which is builded with great stones...' includes הִיא to emphasize the ongoing and successful work in the hands of the builders. Here, the pronoun serves to affirm the reality and progress of the temple construction, underscoring God's providential involvement. It reminds readers that this work is not merely human effort but carries divine approval and blessing, encouraging faith in God's sustaining power.
